claim: Properdin stabilizes convertases formed upon activation of the complement cascade within the immune system.
source: Properdin stabilizes convertases formed upon activation of the complement cascade within the immune system.
evidence: This is a well-established function of properdin stated in the abstract and supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The biological activity of properdin depends on the oligomerization state.
source: The biological activity of properdin depends on the oligomerization state
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and cited literature.

claim: Properdin oligomers adopt extended rigid and well-defined conformations which are well approximated by single models of apparent n-fold rotational symmetry with dimensions of 230–360 Å.
source: We show by combining electron microscopy and solution scattering, that properdin oligomers adopt extended rigid and well-defined conformations which are well approximated by single models of apparent n-fold rotational symmetry with dimensions of 230–360 Å.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by EM and SAXS data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Properdin monomers are pretzel-shaped molecules with limited flexibility.
source: Properdin monomers are pretzel-shaped molecules with limited flexibility.
evidence: This is supported by EM 2D classes in Figure 1B and MD simulations in Figure 1F-G.

claim: In solution, properdin dimers are curved molecules.
source: In solution, properdin dimers are curved molecules
evidence: This is supported by SAXS data and rigid-body modeling presented in Figure 3A.

claim: Properdin trimers and tetramers are close to being planar molecules.
source: whereas trimers and tetramers are close to being planar molecules.
evidence: This is supported by EM 2D classes in Figure 2C,E and SAXS models in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Simultaneous binding through all binding sites to surface-linked convertases is unlikely for properdin trimer and tetramers.
source: Structural analysis indicates that simultaneous binding through all binding sites to surface-linked convertases is unlikely for properdin trimer and tetramers.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the angle α between convertase binding sites, presented in Figure 3F.

claim: Multivalency alone is insufficient for full activity in a cell lysis assay.
source: We show that multivalency alone is insufficient for full activity in a cell lysis assay.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with nanobody-linked FPc oligomers in Figure 5C.

claim: The observed rigid extended oligomer structure is an integral component of properdin function.
source: Hence, the observed rigid extended oligomer structure is an integral component of properdin function.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combination of structural data and functional assays.

claim: The complement system is an essential aspect of innate immunity providing a first line of defense against invading pathogens as well as maintenance of host homeostasis.
source: The complement system is an essential aspect of innate immunity providing a first line of defense against invading pathogens as well as maintenance of host homeostasis.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the complement system.

claim: The complement cascade is activated when circulating pattern recognition molecules recognize molecular patterns on a pathogen, dying host cells, or immune complexes.
source: The complement cascade is activated when circulating pattern recognition molecules recognize molecular patterns on a pathogen, dying host cells, or immune complexes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about complement activation.

claim: Activation can initiate through the classical pathway, the lectin pathway, or the alternative pathway where the AP also provides an amplification loop for the two other pathways.
source: Activation can initiate through the classical pathway, the lectin pathway, or the alternative pathway (AP) where the AP also provides an amplification loop for the two other pathways (Bajic et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bajic et al., 2015.

claim: In all three pathways, labile protein complexes known as C3 and C5 convertases are assembled.
source: In all three pathways, labile protein complexes known as C3 and C5 convertases are assembled.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the complement cascade.

claim: Convertases conduct proteolytic cleavage of complement components C3 and C5, respectively, resulting in the generation of opsonins (C3b and iC3b), anaphylatoxins (C3a and C5a), and assembly of the membrane attack complex.
source: These convertases conduct proteolytic cleavage of complement components C3 and C5, respectively, resulting in the generation of opsonins (C3b and iC3b), anaphylatoxins (C3a and C5a), and assembly of the membrane attack complex (reviewed in Bajic et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bajic et al., 2015.

claim: In the AP, the C3-convertase C3bBb is formed when a complex between C3b and the serine protease factor B (FB) is activated by factor D.
source: In the AP, the C3-convertase C3bBb is formed when a complex between C3b and the serine protease factor B (FB) is activated by factor D.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the alternative pathway.

claim: At a high surface density of C3b, the C3 convertase becomes a C5 convertase.
source: At a high surface density of C3b, this C3 convertase becomes a C5 convertase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about convertase formation.

claim: Properdin (FP) is a positive regulator of these convertases.
source: Properdin (FP) is a positive regulator of these convertases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about properdin function.

claim: FP is a 53 kDa protein composed of an N-terminal TGF-β binding (TB) domain followed by six thrombospondin type I repeats (TSR1-6).
source: FP is a 53 kDa protein composed of an N-terminal TGF-β binding (TB) domain followed by six thrombospondin type I repeats (TSR1-6).
evidence: This is established structural information about properdin.

claim: The protein is heavily post-translationally modified carrying one N-linked glycan, four O-linked glycans, and 14–17 C-mannosylated tryptophan residues in the WxxW motifs present in TSR1-6.
source: The protein is heavily post-translationally modified carrying one N-linked glycan, four O-linked glycans, and 14–17 C-mannosylated tryptophan residues in the WxxW motifs present in TSR1-6 (Pedersen et al., 2019a; van den Bos et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pedersen et al., 2019a and van den Bos et al., 2019.

claim: FP is produced predominantly by monocytes, T cells, and neutrophils.
source: FP is produced predominantly by monocytes, T cells, and neutrophils
evidence: This is established knowledge about properdin production.

claim: FP circulates as oligomers and is primarily found as dimers, trimers, and tetramers with a 1:2:1 molar distribution in plasma at a concentration of 4–25 μg/mL.
source: and circulates as oligomers and is primarily found as dimers, trimers, and tetramers with a 1:2:1 molar distribution in plasma at a concentration of 4–25 μg/mL (Blatt et al., 2016; Pangburn, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Blatt et al., 2016 and Pangburn, 1989.

claim: FP enhances the recruitment of FB to C3b and thereby stimulates proconvertase assembly.
source: (1) FP enhances the recruitment of FB to C3b and thereby stimulates proconvertase assembly
evidence: This is a well-established function of properdin supported by citations.

claim: FP slows the dissociation of C3bBb 5- to 10-fold.
source: (2) FP slows the dissociation of C3bBb 5- to 10-fold
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pedersen et al., 2019a; Pedersen et al., 2017; DiScipio, 1981; Fearon and Austen, 1975.

claim: FP directly competes with factor I resulting in decreased irreversible degradation of C3b to iC3b.
source: (3) FP directly competes with factor I resulting in decreased irreversible degradation of C3b to iC3b (Pedersen et al., 2019a; Pedersen et al., 2017; DiScipio, 1981; Fearon and Austen, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pedersen et al., 2019a; Pedersen et al., 2017; DiScipio, 1981; Fearon and Austen, 1975.

claim: FP can act as a C3b-independent pattern recognition molecule capable of triggering the AP.
source: Other suggested functions of FP are as a C3b-independent pattern recognition molecule capable of triggering the AP (reviewed in Blatt et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Blatt et al., 2016.

claim: FP acts as a ligand for the NKp46 receptor on innate lymphoid cells.
source: and as a ligand for the NKp46 receptor on innate lymphoid cells (Narni-Mancinelli et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Narni-Mancinelli et al., 2017.

claim: Individuals with FP deficiency (PD) demonstrate the importance of FP in innate immunity and homeostasis.
source: The importance of FP in innate immunity and homeostasis is demonstrated by individuals with FP deficiency (PD).
evidence: This is supported by clinical observations and citations.

claim: PD is a rare X-linked disorder, which can be divided into three subtypes: type I (complete lack of FP), type II (1–10% of normal plasma FP level), and type III (normal plasma level but dysfunctional FP).
source: PD is a rare X-linked disorder, which can be divided into three subtypes: type I (complete lack of FP), type II (1–10% of normal plasma FP level), and type III (normal plasma level but dysfunctional FP).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about properdin deficiency.

claim: All PD types are characterized by reduced AP activity, resulting in impaired bactericidal activity and increased susceptibility to Neisseria infections and sepsis.
source: All PD types are characterized by reduced AP activity, resulting in impaired bactericidal activity and increased susceptibility to Neisseria infections and sepsis (Skattum et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Skattum et al., 2011.

claim: Classic negative-stain EM studies of FP dimers, trimers, and tetramers revealed that FP oligomers contain compact eye-shaped vertexes connected by thin connecting structures.
source: Classic negative-stain EM (nsEM) studies of FP dimers, trimers, and tetramers revealed that FP oligomers contain compact eye-shaped vertexes connected by thin connecting structures (Smith et al., 1984; Higgins et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Smith et al., 1984 and Higgins et al., 1995.

claim: Alcorlo and coworkers presented the first 3D reconstruction of the FP eye-shaped vertices in oligomers and 2D classes of the FP-C3bBb convertase complex.
source: Alcorlo and coworkers presented the first 3D reconstruction of the FP eye-shaped vertices in oligomers and 2D classes of the FP-C3bBb convertase complex (Alcorlo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Alcorlo et al., 2013.

claim: Crystal structures demonstrated that FP oligomers are formed upon interaction of the TB domain and TSR1 from one FP monomer with TSR4, TSR5, and TSR6 from a second FP monomer.
source: Recently, crystal structures Pedersen et al., 2019a; van den Bos et al., 2019 demonstrated that FP oligomers are formed upon interaction of the TB domain and TSR1 from one FP monomer with TSR4, TSR5, and TSR6 from a second FP monomer (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pedersen et al., 2019a and van den Bos et al., 2019, and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The binding site for C3b is formed by FP TSR5 in conjunction with a large loop from TSR6.
source: In addition, it was established that the binding site for C3b is formed by FP TSR5 in conjunction with a large loop from TSR6 (Pedersen et al., 2019a; van den Bos et al., 2019; Pedersen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pedersen et al., 2019a; van den Bos et al., 2019; Pedersen et al., 2017.

claim: FP1 is a flat pretzel-shaped molecule with apparent overall projected dimensions of 95 × 115 Å containing a small and a large ring-shaped structure sharing one edge.
source: The resulting 2D classes revealed a flat pretzel-shaped molecule with apparent overall projected dimensions of 95 × 115 Å containing a small and a large ring-shaped structure sharing one edge (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by EM 2D classes shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The small ring of the FP1 molecule corresponds to the well-described FP 'eye' formed by the TB domain, TSR1, TSR5, and TSR6.
source: The small ring of the FP1 molecule corresponds to the well-described FP 'eye' formed by the TB domain, TSR1, TSR5, and TSR6 (Pedersen et al., 2019a; van den Bos et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pedersen et al., 2019a and van den Bos et al., 2019.

claim: The larger ring of FP1 is formed by TSR2, TSR3, and TSR4 together with the TB domain and TSR1.
source: whereas the larger ring is formed by TSR2, TSR3, and TSR4 together with the TB domain and TSR1.
evidence: This is inferred from the EM 2D classes and domain assignment.

claim: Rigid-body refinement of FP1 E244K against SAXS data resulted in models that fitted the data with χ2 = 1.6.
source: The resulting models clustered tightly and fitted the data with χ2 = 1.6 (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E with the fit to experimental SAXS data.

claim: The p(r) function derived from SAXS data on the FP E244K monomer approaches zero at about 130 Å with a small-tail stretching out to a Dmax at 150 Å.
source: The p(r) function derived from our published SAXS data on the FP E244K monomer (Pedersen et al., 2017) approaches zero at about 130 Å with a small-tail stretching out to a Dmax at 150 Å (see insert to Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown in the insert to Figure 1E.

claim: The maximum extent of 140 Å in the nsEM 2D class projections agrees with the SAXS-derived Dmax.
source: This agrees with the maximum extent of 140 Å in the nsEM 2D class projections.
evidence: This is a comparison between SAXS and EM data.

claim: The SAXS curve calculated from the ensemble of conformations sampled by molecular dynamics simulations is in good agreement with the experimental SAXS data (χ2 = 2.2).
source: The SAXS curve calculated from the ensemble of conformations sampled by molecular dynamics simulations is in good agreement with the experimental SAXS data (χ2 = 2.2).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the MD simulation results.

claim: By using experimental data to guide the refinement of the conformational ensemble, the fit could be further improved to χ2 = 1.4 using the Bayesian maximum entropy (BME) method.
source: By using experimental data to guide the refinement of the conformational ensemble, the fit could be further improved to χ2 = 1.4 using the Bayesian maximum entropy (BME) method (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1G with the BME-refined fit.

claim: Two independent MD simulations together suggested that TSR3 inserted between TSR2 and TSR4 is capable of rotating as a rigid body with limited conformational flexibility within domain.
source: However, two independent MD simulations together suggested that TSR3 inserted between TSR2 and TSR4 is capable of rotating as a rigid body with limited conformational flexibility within domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The TSR4 loop region Asn285-Phe295 facing TSR3 exhibits high mobility.
source: This domain rotation was apparently facilitated by high mobility of the TSR4 loop region Asn285-Phe295 facing TSR3, which is in excellent agreement with weak electron density we observed for this region in two crystal structures (Pedersen et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulations and crystal structure observations cited to Pedersen et al., 2019a.

claim: The TSR3 loop Ser225-Pro237 facing TSR2 exhibits flexibility.
source: At the TSR2–TSR3 junction, the corresponding TSR3 loop Ser225-Pro237 facing TSR2 likewise exhibited flexibility (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D and Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The two loops in TSR5 and TSR6 involved in convertase recognition did not exhibit significant changes in backbone conformation during MD simulation.
source: in particular the two loops in TSR5 and TSR6 involved in convertase recognition (Pedersen et al., 2019a; van den Bos et al., 2019) did not exhibit significant changes in backbone conformation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and citations to Pedersen et al., 2019a and van den Bos et al., 2019.

claim: Of the 51% of FP2 particles that were classified, 8/10 appeared in similar 2D classes, suggesting that a limited number of related elliptical dimer conformations are present on the EM grids.
source: Of the 51% of particles that were classified, 8/10 appeared in similar 2D classes, suggesting that a limited number of related elliptical dimer conformations are present on the EM grids (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on EM 2D classification results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The overall projected dimension of FP2 in a typical 2D class was 270 × 130 Å with an inner opening of 110 × 50 Å.
source: The overall projected dimension of FP2 in a typical 2D class was 270 × 130 Å with an inner opening of 110 × 50 Å.
evidence: This is measured from EM 2D classes.

claim: TSR3 of FP2 appeared to connect TSR2 and TSR4 in an almost linear arrangement.
source: Interestingly, TSR3 of FP2 appeared to connect TSR2 and TSR4 in an almost linear arrangement (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is observed in EM 2D classes shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The 2D classes suggested that the two monomers in FP2 are related by an approximate twofold rotation axis (C2 symmetry) perpendicular to the plane of the dimer.
source: The 2D classes suggested that the two monomers in FP2 are related by an approximate twofold rotation axis (C2 symmetry) perpendicular to the plane of the dimer.
evidence: This is inferred from the symmetry observed in EM 2D classes.

claim: When hFPNb1 was included, radically different 2D classes of FP2 were obtained where FP2 appeared as a folded dimer adopting a double-pretzel structure with a maximum dimension of 210 Å.
source: Whereas the FP2 2D classes above concurred with prior EM studies (Smith et al., 1984; Alcorlo et al., 2013), radically different 2D classes were also obtained when hFPNb1 was included (Figure 2B). In one extreme 2D class, FP2 appeared as a folded dimer adopting a double-pretzel structure with a maximum dimension of 210 Å
evidence: This is shown in EM 2D classes in Figure 2B.

claim: In the folded FP2 conformation with hFPNb1, the two connecting arms are crossing over at TSR3, and the TSR2–TSR3 angle is sharply bent.
source: where the two connecting arms are crossing over at TSR3, and like in FP1, the TSR2–TSR3 angle is sharply bent (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is observed in EM 2D classes shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The folded FP2 conformation appeared to have a C2 symmetry axis lying in the plane of the molecule.
source: This FP2 conformation appeared to have a C2 symmetry axis lying in the plane of the molecule in contrast to unbound FP2 where the apparent C2 axis was perpendicular to the plane of the molecule.
evidence: This is inferred from the symmetry observed in EM 2D classes.

claim: A comparison of the SEC profiles supported significant conformational effects of hFPNb1 on FP2 in solution prior to EM sample preparation.
source: A comparison of the SEC profiles supported significant conformational effects of hFPNb1 on FP2 in solution prior to EM sample preparation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in SEC profiles in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: hFPNb1 does not influence the oligomer distribution.
source: Importantly, hFPNb1 does not influence the oligomer distribution as shown previously (Pedersen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pedersen et al., 2020.

claim: Eight very similar 2D classes of FP3 contained >90% of the particles picked.
source: We next analyzed the properdin trimer (FP3) by nsEM, where eight very similar 2D classes contained >90% of the particles picked (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on EM 2D classification results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In FP3 2D classes, FP3 appeared in projection as flat triangular molecules with pseudo-C3 symmetry having maximum edges of 280 Å with mainly straight connections formed by TSR2, TSR3, and TSR4 between the vertices.
source: In these classes, FP3 appeared in projection as flat triangular molecules with pseudo-C3 symmetry having maximum edges of 280 Å with mainly straight connections formed by TSR2, TSR3, and TSR4 between the vertices.
evidence: This is observed in EM 2D classes shown in Figure 2C.

claim: When hFPNb1 was present with FP3, some 2D classes contained a less planar FP3 with a maximal dimension of 240 Å.
source: Again, when hFPNb1 was present, some 2D classes contained a less planar FP3 with a maximal dimension of 240 Å where only the eye-shaped vertices could be unambiguously identified (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in EM 2D classes in Figure 2D.

claim: >90% of the picked FP4 particles contributed to 2D classes with flat molecules of pseudo-C4 symmetry with a maximum extent of 380 Å.
source: Finally, we analyzed the properdin tetramer (FP4) by nsEM and again >90% of the picked particles contributed to 2D classes with flat molecules of pseudo-C4 symmetry with a maximum extent of 380 Å (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on EM 2D classification results shown in Figure 2E.

claim: For both FP3 and FP4 2D classes, a kink was occasionally observed, presumably at the TSR2–TSR3 interface, in at least one of the TSR2–TSR3–TSR4 connections.
source: For both FP3 and FP4 2D classes, a kink was occasionally observed, presumably at the TSR2–TSR3 interface, in at least one of the TSR2–TSR3–TSR4 connections.
evidence: This is observed in EM 2D classes.

claim: The sum of particles used for the 2D classes for all three oligomers represented at least 50% of the particles picked.
source: Furthermore, the oligomer conformations observed in our 2D classes were not rare since the sum of particles used for the 2D classes for all three oligomers represented at least 50% of the particles picked (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by particle counts in Figure 2.

claim: The TSR4-specific hFPNb1 could induce alternative folded conformations of the TSR2–TSR3–TSR4 arms in FP2 and FP3 that appeared to be in equilibrium through intermediates with their elliptical and flat triangular conformations.
source: Intriguingly, we also observed that the TSR4-specific hFPNb1 could induce alternative folded conformations of the TSR2–TSR3–TSR4 arms in FP2 and FP3 that appeared to be in equilibrium through intermediates with their elliptical and flat triangular conformations.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of multiple conformations in EM 2D classes with hFPNb1.

claim: The SAXS data of all three oligomers exhibit characteristic bumps, which are also reflected in their p(r) functions.
source: It is noteworthy that the SAXS data of all three oligomers exhibit characteristic bumps, which are also reflected in their p(r) functions (see inserts to SAXS data and Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is shown in the SAXS data and p(r) functions in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The presence of pronounced features in SAXS data clearly indicates that the oligomers are rather rigid and well defined.
source: The presence of these pronounced features clearly indicates that the oligomers are rather rigid and well defined.
evidence: This is inferred from the characteristics of the SAXS data.

claim: If conformational freedom had been present, this would smear out the SAXS data.
source: If conformational freedom had been present, this would smear out the SAXS data.
evidence: This is a theoretical consideration about SAXS data interpretation.

claim: The p(r) functions of FP1, FP2, FP3, and FP4 all exhibit an initial bump at around 40 Å corresponding well to the repeated distance across the eye.
source: The p(r) functions of FP1, FP2, FP3, and FP4 all exhibit an initial bump at around 40 Å corresponding well to the repeated distance across the eye that is also visible in the nsEM pictures of all three oligomers (Figures 1B and 2).
evidence: This is observed in the p(r) functions and correlated with EM images.

claim: The FP2 has a Dmax value of 230 Å.
source: The FP2 has a Dmax value of 230 Å.
evidence: This is derived from SAXS data analysis.

claim: The FP2 p(r) has a second well-defined peak at around 80 Å, which is most likely related to the distance between the two antiparallel arms connecting the two eyes.
source: Along with a second well-defined peak at around 80 Å, which is most likely related to the distance between the two antiparallel arms connecting the two eyes
evidence: This is inferred from the p(r) function and structural knowledge.

claim: The Dmax value of FP2 indicates that the FP2 solution structure is in better agreement with the extended conformation of FP2 than with the more compact twisted conformation induced by hFPNb1.
source: the Dmax value indicates that the FP2 solution structure is in better agreement with the extended conformation of FP2 (Figure 2A), than it is with the more compact twisted conformation induced by hFPNb1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the Dmax value with the dimensions observed in EM 2D classes.

claim: The p(r) of FP2 has a broad peak at 165 Å corresponding well to the distance between the two eyes.
source: Finally, the p(r) of FP2 has a broad peak at 165 Å corresponding well to the distance between the two eyes.
evidence: This is observed in the p(r) function and correlated with structural features.

claim: The Dmax of the FP3 and FP4 p(r) functions are, respectively, 250 and 360 Å.
source: The Dmax of the FP3 and FP4 p(r) functions are, respectively, 250 and 360 Å (Figure 3B,C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1H)
evidence: This is derived from SAXS data analysis shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The Dmax values of FP3 and FP4 are in good agreement with their larger sizes also seen in the nsEM 2D classes.
source: and in good agreement with their larger sizes also seen in the nsEM 2D classes (Figure 2C,E).
evidence: This is a comparison between SAXS and EM data.

claim: For the FP3 and FP4, the p(r) middle peak at around 80–100 Å appears broader, less pronounced, and moves to higher values as the oligomer size increases.
source: For the FP3 and FP4, the p(r) middle peak at around 80–100 Å appears broader, less pronounced, and moves to higher values as the oligomer size increases.
evidence: This is observed in the p(r) functions.

claim: FP3 and FP4 have a high p(r) peak at 180 and 195 Å, respectively, which is most likely the result of neighbor eye–eye distances.
source: FP3 and FP4 have a high p(r) peak at 180 and 195 Å, respectively, which is most likely the result of neighbor eye–eye distances.
evidence: This is inferred from the p(r) functions and structural knowledge.

claim: The increase of the eye–eye peak position when comparing FP2, FP3, and FP4 suggests that the eyes organize in a more planar structure as the oligomerization increases.
source: The increase of the eye–eye peak position when comparing FP2, FP3, and FP4 suggests that the eyes organize in a more planar structure as the oligomerization increases.
evidence: This is inferred from the trend in p(r) functions.

claim: The FP4 p(r) function exhibits an additional small shoulder at 280 Å, which corresponds well to the less-frequent diagonal eye–eye distances.
source: Furthermore, the FP4 p(r) function exhibits an additional small shoulder at 280 Å, which corresponds well to the less-frequent diagonal eye–eye distances.
evidence: This is observed in the p(r) function and correlated with the expected geometry.

claim: For a quadratic structure, diagonal eye–eye distances would appear at √2 times the position of the neighbor eye–eye distances at 180–195 Å as they indeed do.
source: For a quadratic structure, as suggested by the nsEM, these would appear at √2 times the position of the neighbor eye–eye distances at 180–195 Å as they indeed do.
evidence: This is a geometric calculation that matches the observed p(r) function.

claim: Rigid-body models of FP2 were obtained with χ2 in the range 1.4–3.0 for C1 symmetry, whereas models with C2 symmetry had χ2 of 2.4–5.5.
source: we obtained rigid-body models of FP2 in the presence of C1 (no) symmetry or a C2 symmetry axis with χ2 in the range 1.4–3.0 for C1 symmetry, whereas models with C2 symmetry had χ2 of 2.4–5.5 (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The resulting SAXS-based FP2 models all featured an extended FP2 conformation rather than the double-pretzel FP2 observed by nsEM.
source: The resulting SAXS-based FP2 models all featured an extended FP2 conformation rather than the double-pretzel FP2 observed by nsEM
evidence: This is stated in the text comparing SAXS models to EM observations.

claim: The FP2 SAXS models appeared more curved as compared to the extended conformations present in EM 2D classes.
source: Interestingly, the FP2 SAXS models appeared more curved as compared to the extended conformations present in EM 2D classes.
evidence: This is a comparison between SAXS models and EM 2D classes.

claim: In contrast to the nsEM 2D classes, the rigid-body models of FP2 cannot be projected such that the two eye shapes at the opposite ends of FP2 become visible simultaneously.
source: In contrast to the nsEM 2D classes, the rigid-body models cannot be projected such that the two eye shapes at the opposite ends of FP2 become visible simultaneously.
evidence: This is a comparison between SAXS models and EM 2D classes.

claim: For FP3 and FP4, the χ2 values for the fit of the best models to the experimental data were comparable and in the range 1.1–1.4.
source: In contrast to FP2, the χ2 values for the fit of the best models to the experimental data were comparable and in the range 1.1–1.4
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the SAXS modeling results.

claim: The χ2 values of the output models generated with C3/C4 symmetry were similar to those generated with C1 symmetry demonstrating that the fit to the data was independent of symmetry.
source: Importantly, the χ2 values of the output models generated with C3/C4 symmetry were similar to those generated with C1 symmetry demonstrating that the fit to the data was independent of symmetry (Figure 3B,C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: All FP3 and FP4 models generated with C1 symmetry were qualitatively similar extended circularized structures with their three or four eye-shaped structures joined by peripheral TSR2–TSR3–TSR4 connecting arms.
source: All models generated with C1 symmetry were qualitatively similar extended circularized structures with their three or four eye-shaped structures joined by peripheral TSR2–TSR3–TSR4 connecting arms in agreement with the FP3 and FP4 nsEM 2D classes.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the SAXS models.

claim: For FP3 and FP4 SAXS models generated with C1 symmetry, it was never possible to obtain projections in which all eyes were visible.
source: As for FP2, in the models generated with C1 symmetry, it was never possible to obtain projections of these SAXS models in which all eyes in FP3 and FP4 were visible.
evidence: This is stated in the text comparing SAXS models to EM observations.

claim: For some FP3 and FP4 models generated with C3/C4 symmetry, it was possible to visualize all eyes simultaneously in projections.
source: For some of these models, it was possible to visualize all eyes simultaneously in projections (Figure 3B,C)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: The average solution conformation of FP3 and FP4 are well approximated by single models with C3 and C4 symmetry.
source: Overall, our SAXS analysis of FP oligomers were in agreement with the corresponding nsEM 2D classes and suggests that the average solution conformation of FP3 and FP4 are well approximated by single models with C3 and C4 symmetry (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
